titre: La Rinconada, the Highest City in the World, and Its Thicker Blood
accroche: At 5,100 meters, the air carries half as much oxygen as at sea level. The residents don't simply survive there: their blood has changed.
contenu_vulgarise:
La Rinconada, in Peru, clings to the slopes of Mount Ananea between 4,900 and 5,100 meters in altitude. It is the highest permanently inhabited settlement in the world, born from a gold prospectors' camp and grown into a city of several thousand people, with no running water or sewers. At this height, the air contains about half as much oxygen as at sea level, enough to leave a visitor breathless on a simple flight of stairs. Its residents, for their part, live, work, and sleep there year after year.

## The Mechanism

Faced with chronic oxygen shortage, the human body has two strategies: breathe faster, which is exhausting in the long run, or carry more oxygen in each breath by making more red blood cells. The second route is the one taken by Andean populations settled at very high altitude for generations.

A study published in 2020 in the journal Frontiers in Physiology, conducted among 1,594 adults in La Rinconada, measured the scale of the phenomenon: 44.1% of residents exceed the international threshold for “excessive erythrocytosis,” a hematocrit level judged abnormally high (63% in men, 57% in women). One resident in seven also shows symptoms of chronic mountain sickness, measured by a standardized international questionnaire: shortness of breath, sleep disturbances, headaches, ringing in the ears. In the great majority of cases, these symptoms remain mild.

## The Shift

The study's most surprising result reverses the common intuition. One would expect the residents with the thickest blood to also be the most affected: the opposite was observed, with those who exceed the international threshold for excessive erythrocytosis reporting on average fewer symptoms than the others.

The explanation lies in the threshold itself: the international criteria were established from Andean populations living between 4,000 and 4,300 meters, not at 5,100. Applying a threshold recalculated directly on the La Rinconada population (72% in men, 68% in women), the proportion judged “excessive” falls to 13.4%. The same blood sample, measured with two different rulers, thus changes diagnosis depending on the reference altitude the physician adopts. What altitude shifts is not only the composition of the blood: it is the very definition of what a healthy human body should contain.

repere.texte: Of 1,594 adults studied in La Rinconada (4,900-5,100 m), 44.1% exceed the international threshold for excessive erythrocytosis, but those who exceed it report on average fewer symptoms than the others.
repere.source: Hancco et al., Frontiers in Physiology, 2020

carte.punch: At 5,100 meters, having “too many” red blood cells may not be a problem.
carte.idee: La Rinconada, in Peru, is the highest city in the world, at about 5,000 m, where the air carries half as much oxygen as at sea level. The body adapts by making more red blood cells, to the point that 44% of residents exceed the international threshold judged excessive.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Excessive Erythrocytosis and Chronic Mountain Sickness in Dwellers of the Highest City in the World (Frontiers in Physiology, 2020)

quiz.question: Why is a high red blood cell level not necessarily a sign of a health problem in La Rinconada?
choix: Because residents drink a mineral water that skews blood measurements
Because the “excessive” threshold used worldwide is calibrated on a lower altitude, around 4,000-4,300 m
Because local doctors refuse to apply the international diagnostic criteria
Because altitude artificially reduces the size of red blood cells measured in the lab
quiz.explication: The international threshold for excessive erythrocytosis was established from populations living between 4,000 and 4,300 m. At La Rinconada, higher still, the study shows that residents who exceed it report on average fewer symptoms of chronic mountain sickness than the others: which suggests that this threshold does not apply as is to extreme altitude.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What are the two strategies available to the human body in the face of chronic oxygen shortage at high altitude?
choix: Breathe faster, or make more red blood cells
Reduce physical activity, or drink much more water
Sleep longer, or eat a diet richer in iron
Migrate to a lower altitude, or wear an oxygen mask
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text distinguishes two strategies in the face of chronic oxygen shortage: breathing faster, which is exhausting in the long run, or making more red blood cells to carry more oxygen.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which result of the 2020 study goes against common intuition?
choix: Women have a higher hematocrit level than men in La Rinconada
Hematocrit level decreases with age among the city's residents
Residents with the thickest blood report on average fewer symptoms than the others
Passing visitors suffer less from altitude sickness than residents
quiz_supplementaire.explication: One would expect the residents with the thickest blood to be the most affected; the study observes the opposite, with those who exceed the threshold reporting on average fewer symptoms.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What proportion of the residents studied show symptoms of chronic mountain sickness, and how are they measured?
choix: Nearly all residents, via a mandatory blood test
Fewer than one resident in a hundred, via an in-depth genetic study
Half of residents, via a non-standardized self-reported survey
About one resident in seven, via a standardized international questionnaire
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The study measures symptoms with a standardized international questionnaire and finds that one resident in seven shows them, most often in a mild form.
